output.summary: C9orf72 hexanucleotide repeat expansion is the most common known genetic cause of familial frontotemporal dementia and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Median survival in C9orf72-FTD is approximately 8–10 years from symptom onset. Motor neuron disease features (upper and lower motor neuron signs) develop in approximately 10–15% of cases. The expansion follows autosomal dominant inheritance with high penetrance; first-degree relatives have a 50% risk of carrying the mutation.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not start acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine): no benefit in FTD and may worsen behavioral symptoms.
Do not start memantine: no evidence of benefit in bvFTD and may worsen behavioral symptoms.
Avoid antipsychotics as first-line behavioral therapy given increased cerebrovascular and mortality risk in dementia; reserve for refractory dangerous agitation with specialist oversight.
Avoid benzodiazepines for behavioral control: risk of paradoxical disinhibition and falls.
required_recommendations: Given C9orf72 expansion, screen actively for ALS features at every visit (FVC, fasciculations, dysarthria, bulbar symptoms).
Initiate genetic counselling and discuss cascade testing for at-risk relatives.
Apply Rascovsky 2011 bvFTD criteria explicitly (≥3 of 6 core features within 3 years) and document functional decline.
Assess and document decision-making, financial, and driving capacity given the high risk of impulsivity and impaired judgment in FTD.
Provide caregiver education, safety planning, and referral to FTD-focused support resources.
Offer genetic counselling and discuss cascade testing options if a pathogenic variant is identified or suspected.

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG is non-specific in FTD; not part of the standard dementia workup unless seizures or rapidly progressive course suggest CJD or autoimmune encephalitis.
ECG has no role in the cognitive workup of suspected FTD; reserved for syncope, palpitations, or pre-procedure clearance.
Echocardiography is unrelated to a neurodegenerative cognitive syndrome and adds cost without diagnostic value.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is unrelated to FTD and not indicated absent syncope or palpitations.
Non-contrast head CT lacks the resolution and lobar specificity needed to characterise frontotemporal atrophy; MRI is the standard structural study.
MR spectroscopy has no established role in the routine FTD diagnostic pathway.
Perfusion MRI is not indicated in the standard FTD workup once a structural MRI and FDG-PET (or amyloid PET) have characterised the lobar pattern.
Carotid duplex is a vascular study with no diagnostic role in primary neurodegenerative dementia.
DaTscan evaluates presynaptic dopaminergic terminals; it is not indicated unless overt parkinsonism raises concern for PD, DLB, or atypical parkinsonism (PSP/CBS overlap).

accepted: Behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD), probable, familial

differential.key_features: AD can present with behavioral features; amyloid PET and the frontal-predominant FDG pattern argue against.
C9orf72 confers high risk of comorbid ALS; warrants careful motor exam, surveillance for fasciculations/dysarthria/weakness.
Family history of paternal personality change with early death is consistent with familial FTD rather than psychiatric illness.
Although construction-worker demographic could carry alcohol exposure, imaging and behavioural pattern fit a primary neurodegenerative syndrome.
No vascular risk-driven imaging pattern; lobar atrophy and FDG hypometabolism are the dominant findings.

key_clinical_evidence: Behavioural Rascovsky criteria met with frontotemporal MRI/FDG pattern.
C9orf72 expansion identified — informs prognosis (faster decline, ALS risk) and cascade family testing.
Mild rigidity is not parkinsonism warranting DaTscan; lobar imaging pattern is diagnostic.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Mild extrapyramidal features are seen in advanced bvFTD without warranting nigrostriatal imaging.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Could prompt DaTscan for suspected parkinsonism.

clinical_assessment.impression: 3 of the six Rascovsky behavioural features are documented, against the three required for possible behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia, alongside a dysexecutive bedside profile. The diagnosis is behavioural and is made on this assessment; imaging supports it and does not substitute for it. Memory and visuospatial function are relatively spared, which is the discriminator against Alzheimer's disease and the reason a screening total alone understates the syndrome.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. T. is a 55-year-old right-handed Black man referred by his primary care physician for progressive behavioral changes over the past 2 years. His wife describes a gradual but unmistakable change in his personality. Previously respected as a firm but fair foreman, he began exhibiting unpredictable behavior at work: making crude jokes in safety briefings, verbally harassing coworkers, and ignoring safety protocols that he had enforced for 20 years. Eight months ago, following a workplace incident where he made physical contact with a coworker in an inappropriate manner, he was placed on administrative leave. At home, his behavior has also deteriorated: he argues viciously with his teenage children over trivial issues, has impulsively purchased a motorcycle despite their financial concerns, and has begun eating voraciously — consuming his children's food off their plates. His wife notes he shows no remorse for any of these behaviors and seems almost amused when confronted. He has developed fixed routines, insisting on watching the same news program at the same time each day and becoming agitated when interrupted. He denies all behavioral problems. Family history is notable for his father's personality change and early death around age 62.
